axes.model_access:
**Official line: optimized for Gemini, but it is also model-agnostic.**

README **verbatim**: "While optimized for Gemini, ADK is **model-agnostic**,
deployment-agnostic, and compatible with
other frameworks."

**So non-Gemini models can be connected.** The official "Models for Agents" page gives three integration mechanisms:

- **① direct string / registry** — Gemini, Claude, Agent Platform hosted models
- **② model connectors** — `LiteLlm` / `ApigeeLlm` wrapper classes
- **③ model routing** — runtime dynamic model selection + automatic failover

**Official wording**: "providing a standardized, OpenAI-compatible interface to over 100+ LLMs"

Local / self-hosted models have dedicated official pages: Ollama, vLLM, LiteRT-LM.

⚠ **Not stated officially**: what "optimized for Gemini" actually optimizes.

⚠ Nor is there a reliability comparison of tool calling and
structured output under non-Gemini models.
**Checked**: the Models page and the LiteLLM page.
axes.runtime:
**Four run forms, all provided by the `adk` CLI or containers (README verified).**

- **① interactive CLI** — `adk run <agent-folder>`
- **② built-in Web UI** — `adk web <agent-folder>`. The official docs state support for
  multi-agent directories or pointing directly at a single agent folder

- **③ Development UI** — the built-in development/debug console
- **④ containerized deployment** — `adk deploy docker --with_ui <agent-folder>`

**Official wording**: "A built-in development UI to help you test, evaluate, debug, and showcase your agent(s)"

⚠ All four are **your local or your cloud processes**. ADK itself provides no hosted service.

Hosting requires Vertex AI Agent Engine or Cloud Run
— those are Google products, not this framework's.
axes.local_files:
**The official answer to "files" is the abstraction layer Artifacts, not the raw filesystem (verified this round).**
In other words, it does not read or write disks itself.

Official Artifacts page **verbatim**:

**Official wording**: Artifacts "represent a crucial mechanism for managing named, versioned binary data associated either with a specific user interaction session or persistently with a user"

**Where things land is decided by the ArtifactService you choose.** **Official wording**: "Their storage and retrieval are managed by a dedicated Artifact Service"

Two backends:

- `InMemoryArtifactService` — lost on restart
- `GcsArtifactService` — persistent, versioned

**ADK is a library; it does not ship Read/Write/Bash style file tools.**
Disk access means writing your own function tool, or connecting MCP.
The official MCP page example is exactly a filesystem MCP server.

⚠ **Not provided officially**: any sandbox mechanism or filesystem permission model (Artifacts, tools, deploy pages checked).
The default access boundary depends on whatever tools you connect.
axes.background:
**It does not host a background. The official docs give two explicit pieces of evidence: session/state persistence, and resume-after-interruption.**

**① Persistence** — SessionService comes in three tiers:

- `InMemorySessionService` — **official wording**:
  "All conversation data is lost if the application restarts"

- `DatabaseSessionService` — "Data survives application restarts"
- `VertexAiSessionService` — hosted

MemoryService separately has InMemory and
Vertex AI Memory Bank tiers.

**② Resume** — ADK Python 1.16+ can configure an App with
`ResumabilityConfig(is_resumable=True)`.

Official **verbatim**:

**Official wording**: "allows an agent workflow to pick up where it left off"

Resume by Invocation ID.
Works via `/run_sse` or `runner.run_async`.

**ADK itself is a library and hosts nothing.** A true background means deploying to Cloud Run /
Vertex AI Agent Engine — that is your cloud resource.

⚠ Two official boundaries:

- Resume is currently "not currently supported" triggered from the Web UI / CLI
- tools may be re-executed (the official docs remind: side-effectful tools need your own dedup)
axes.tools:
**The tool ecosystem is what it emphasizes most, and MCP is a first-class capability in the official docs.**

README **verbatim**:

"Utilize pre-built tools, custom functions,
**OpenAPI specs**, **MCP tools** or
integrate existing tools"

There is also a dedicated MCP tools documentation page.
It provides the `McpToolset` class, and it is **bidirectional**:

- let ADK act as an MCP client, connecting external MCP servers
  (examples include filesystem / Google Maps MCP servers)

- ADK tools can also be wrapped as an MCP server and exposed outward
- transports cover stdio and Streamable HTTP

**Tool-level human confirmation (HITL)** **Official wording**: "a tool confirmation flow (HITL) that can guard tool execution with explicit confirmation and custom input"

Corresponding doc `tools/confirmation`.
Mechanism details in the permissions axis.

**This is a rare "tool-level human confirmation" among objects collected on this site.**
It is a different layer from the OpenAI Agents SDK's input/output guardrail.
axes.context:
**The official docs draw a clear distinction among session / memory, and there is a dedicated context-compaction feature.**

Three sentences on the official sessions page, **official wording**: `Session` is "single, ongoing interaction",
`State` is "data within the current conversation",
`Memory` is "searchable, cross-session information"

The first two are managed by `SessionService`.
Long-term knowledge is managed by `MemoryService`.

**Compaction**: ADK Python 1.16.0+ provides Context Compaction. **Official wording**: "reduce the size of context as an agent is running by summarizing older parts of the agent workflow event history"

The mechanism is a **sliding window**:

- configure `EventsCompactionConfig(compaction_interval, overlap_size)`
- at the threshold, earlier events get summarized
- `summarizer` can swap models

⚠ Per this site's "state ≠ context": `state` governs flow data.
Compaction governs history compression. These are two mechanisms, and the official docs describe them separately.
axes.permissions:
**The officially explicit mechanism is tool-level human confirmation, Tool Confirmation (HITL).**

Doc `tools/confirmation` (since v1.14.0, labeled **Experimental**) **official wording**: "allows an ADK Tool to pause its execution and interact with a user or other system for confirmation"

**Two usage styles verified.**

- **① simple confirmation** — `FunctionTool(..., require_confirmation=True)` asks once yes/no;
  you can also pass a function returning a boolean (e.g. "only ask when amount > 1000")

- **② advanced confirmation** — `tool_context.request_confirmation(hint, payload)`.
  Can pause the tool, collect structured data (e.g. approval days) and then resume

Without a UI, the ADK server's `/run` or
`/run_sse` REST endpoints allow remote confirmation.

**This is only "ask before executing", not boundary-setting.**
The official docs provide no sandbox or filesystem permission model.
**Checked**: confirmation, Artifacts, deploy pages.

⚠ Official known limitation: DatabaseSessionService and
VertexAiSessionService do not support this feature.
axes.fit:
**Fits these cases.**

- organizing multiple agents into a **deterministic flow with branching, loops and human intervention**
- defining agents and tools code-first, for testability and version control
- teams inside the Google ecosystem (Cloud Run / Vertex / Gemini)
- needing built-in eval and a development UI
- wanting one framework covering both Python and TypeScript
- needing tool-level human confirmation, session persistence and resume-after-interruption

**Does not fit these cases.**

- running a single agent only, no graph structure needed — OpenAI Agents SDK or Deep Agents are lighter
- needing framework-built file / network sandbox boundaries — **not provided officially**.
  File access relies on the Artifacts abstraction or tools you connect yourself

- wanting out-of-the-box self-hosted weights without going through the LiteLLM adapter layer

sections.为什么把它归到 orchestration，而不是 coding-base:
This site's first four coding bases are the OpenAI Agents SDK, Deep Agents,
Claude Agent SDK, Codex SDK.

They all answer the same question:

> how do you run one agent?

ADK answers a different question:

> how do you organize multiple agents into a flow with branching, loops and human intervention?

**The keyword is deterministic**: what it sets out to solve is not "whether an agent can work".
(deterministic means "certainty".)

What it sets out to solve is whether a flow composed of multiple **agents** is repeatable and predictable across runs.

This lands directly on the distinction this site cares about:

| The surface this site watches | What ADK gives |
|---|---|
| **state** (flow control) | ✅ graph execution engine: routing / loops / retry / state management / nested workflows |
| **context** (long-task compression) | ✅ Context Compaction since 1.16+: sliding-window summarization of earlier events (`EventsCompactionConfig(compaction_interval, overlap_size)`), `summarizer` swappable |
sections.工具生态：MCP 是其中一员，但量级要注意:
**README verbatim:**

> Utilize pre-built tools, custom functions, **OpenAPI specs**, **MCP tools** or integrate existing tools to give agents diverse capabilities, all for tight integration with the Google ecosystem.

⚠ **This site's judgment (inference; implementation not verified)**: the README lists MCP **alongside** OpenAPI specs.

This suggests it integrates MCP as "one source of tools".

This differs from the [OpenAI Agents SDK](./openai-agents-sdk.md).

That one puts `mcp>=1.19.0,<3` directly in `dependencies`.
That is a framework-level dependency.

**The two are not first-class citizens of the same weight.**

### One official capability worth a separate look: Tool Confirmation (HITL)

> A tool confirmation flow (HITL) that can **guard tool execution with explicit confirmation and custom input**.

The doc is at `tools/confirmation`.

**This is a rare "tool-level human confirmation" among objects collected on this site.**
input/output guardrails are a different layer from it:

- guardrails **validate content** (is this input / output compliant)
- tool confirmation **gates execution** (should this tool really run, optionally with custom input)
sections.部署：四条命令，从本地到 Google 云:
**All four run/deployment forms given by the README are verified:**

```bash
adk run <agent-folder>              # interactive CLI
adk web                <agent-folder>       # built-in Web UI
adk deploy docker   --with_ui <agent-folder>         # containerized
adk deploy cloud_run --with_ui <agent-folder>        # Cloud Run
```

**Two more points this site considers notable.**

**① Built-in development UI and built-in eval.**

**Official wording**:

> A built-in development UI to help you **test, evaluate, debug, and showcase** your agent(s)

**There is also** the `adk eval <agent-folder> <evalset.json>` command and the `.evalset.json` config format.

**This is the only object collected on this site that makes "evaluation" a framework-built-in command.**
Against the "no measured runs" rule, this kind of capability deserves a note: it lets users run their own evaluations.

**② There is a deployment-level switch to note, and it is essentially a "billing-path switch."**

**The README's Cloud Run example contains** `GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_ENTERPRISE=1`.

**Verified clearly this round (2026-10-01, Google's official codelab and Cloud docs)**:
it is **not a switch that "unlocks enterprise features"**.

**It is a routing switch: moving requests from the Gemini Developer API to the Google Cloud enterprise platform
(Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform / Vertex AI), and the billing basis changes with it.**

In other words, what changes is where requests go, not feature entitlements.

**The official codelab's explanation of the three variables, verbatim:**

| Variable | Official meaning |
|---|---|
| `GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_ENTERPRISE` | "This tells the ADK that you intend to use Google's **Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform** service for your Generative AI operations." |
| `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` | "ADK needs this to correctly associate your agent with your cloud resources and **enable billing**." |
| `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` | region, e.g. `global` |

**The single most important line.**

The official docs write "enable billing" explicitly against
`GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`.

**Set all three variables together and the agent lands in your Google Cloud project and starts billing.**
Unset, it goes the Gemini Developer API route (which has its own free tier and quotas).

**Two more points worth recording**:

- **the three variables must appear as a group** — every official example (README, codelab, the Cloud docs'
  Live API guide) sets all three; there is no set-one-only style

- **values are inconsistent** — the README and codelab `.env` files write `1`,
  the Cloud docs write `TRUE` or `True`. All are truthy by boolean semantics, but the official inconsistency itself is worth noting

> ⚠ Still unverified: Gemini's specific unit prices.
> And the actual rates of Vertex AI Agent Engine and Cloud Run.

**If you choose it, container isolation is yours to confirm.**

related: **The pair this site should contrast most**: both are graph-execution orchestration frameworks, and LangGraph's checkpointer / interrupt mechanisms vs ADK's state management + HITL are two answers to the same class of problem. Only after collecting the latter can this site offer an internal comparison of orchestration frameworks.
Both orchestration frameworks, but CrewAI centers on the "roles/tasks/flows" abstraction while ADK centers on "graph nodes" — different abstraction levels.
Both vendor-line frameworks but opposite in form: that one is single-agent primitives (primitives-only); ADK is multi-agent orchestration.

The negative contrast: OpenHands is a scheduling platform with a Web UI that can also attach third-party agents; ADK is a code-first library. Both orchestrate, but one faces the interface and one faces the code.
